newsitem.title: USA: Swiss ambassador says memo was misunderstood.
newsitem.headline: Swiss ambassador says memo was misunderstood.

text.p: The Swiss ambassador to Washington on Friday denied antisemitic intent in writing a leaked memo that forced him to resign, saying he was trying to help resolve a dispute over the wealth of Holocaust victims.

Carlo Jagmetti, outgoing envoy to Washington, told a news conference he had been misunderstood. He said he was not, as angry critics have assumed, attacking Jewish groups who are pressing the Swiss government and banks for an accounting of funds stolen by Nazis from Jews murdered in the Holocaust.
"The allegation of antisemitism is a particularly despicable one that gratuitously offends my longstanding upholding of human values at large," Jagmetti said.

But he added in a long statement defending his motives: "Sensitivities in America or in Switzerland are not identical; the art of communications or the use of language diverge in many respects ... misunderstandings can and unfortunately will arise on occasion."

In the Dec. 19 memo marked "internal and classified," Jagmetti wrote: "We are faced with a war (over the Holocaust wealth issue) which Switzerland must conduct and win abroad and at home. Most of the opponents cannot be trusted."
He announced his resignation on Monday effective at the end of March, saying he could no longer serve effectively amid a furore stirred by the leak of his memo to Swiss newspapers.
He said the "opponents" he referred to were "the vocal minority who criticise Switzerland," adding, "I found great cooperation and understanding among Jewish organisations.

"Whatever harsh words I used in the text of this internal, not for public consumption, confidential document, were meant to energise our decision makers to advance this issue as quickly as possible. My words were and are a call for the Swiss to get our act together," he said in his statement.
"Nothing is more important to the people and government of Switzerland than establishing the complete truth in this matter as swiftly and humanely as possible," Jagmetti said.

He added: "If it is determined that assets that belonged to victims of the Holcaust are still being held in Switzerland, my government will not rest until they are returned to their rightful owners or a relevant charity."
Partly in response to international criticism, Switzerland set up a commission to investigate allegations that Swiss banks are holding the dormant wealth of Nazi victims.
Swiss banks said they have found 38 million Swiss francs in unclaimed accounts, but Jewish groups say they believe the amount is far larger.
In the memo, Jagmetti recommended the Swiss government resolve the matter through international legal measures rather than trying to work out a deal for a lump sum payment to Jewish organisations.

Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican who is leading a congressional investigation of the Swiss accounts, has urged the Swiss government to repudiate Jagmetti's memo. D'Amato has sharply criticised Switzerland's actions.

On Wednesday, New York City and state officals warned Switzerland they would make it difficult for Swiss banks to do business in New York unless the Swiss created a fund to compensate Holcaust victims.
Swiss banks say they are already working fast to set up a Holocaust memorial fund and urged New York politicians to study the facts before deciding on a threatened boycott.
In Geneva on Thursday, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan called Switzerland's dispute with Jews a public relations disaster and urged a fair settlement.
"I hope the issue will be resolved quickly and appropriately and equitably to the satisfaction of all parties concerned," Annan said.
